log.after: Wesgro's six units sit inside a system of fifteen external organisations whose decision rights are split across three spheres of government and industry (Inception Report, Nov 2025, p7, organisations as shown on the stakeholder map and grouped by this report; Current State Diagnostic, Dec 2025, p58). The six units are Cape Town Air Access, Cruise Cape Town, the Convention Bureau, Destination Marketing, Research and Tourism. Between them they cover route development, cruise, business events bids, destination marketing, research and tourism promotion for Cape Town and the Western Cape. The Western Cape Government (Economic Development and Tourism) and the City of Cape Town make up provincial and city government. The provincial tier sets jobs, inclusion and spatial outcomes, runs sector development and safety programmes and plans infrastructure and resilience. The local tier delivers services and manages precincts. It also readies events and place experience and handles congestion, by-laws and community impact. South African Tourism, Airports Company South Africa, Transnet and the South African Maritime Safety Authority sit at the national tier. It holds visa rules and border compliance. It also holds air service agreements and route rights, sets national brand and investment priorities and runs airport capacity and port operations. Cape Town Tourism, the V&A Waterfront, CapeNature, South African National Parks and the Table Mountain Aerial Cableway are the destination and attraction bodies. They carry demand generation and destination marketing as well as product quality and visitor experience at the flagship sites. The private operators, MSC Cruises, Cape Grace, Pullman Hotels and Resorts (Cape Town City Centre) and Southern Sun, carry route and product viability and commercial performance. They also set pricing and service standards. Together they form the industry tier.

log.after: The executive summary gives the case in short: the growth case to 2035, the constraints that cap it, the twenty focus areas by pillar, the first 24 months and the headline indicators. It stands alone, for the Board, Exco and the February 2027 launch audience. Chapter 1 is for every reader, and is the chapter of the body a Board member should read if they read no other. It sets out what Wesgro asked for, where the system stands after recovery, why the next step is constrained by peak capacity and how the study ran. Chapter 2 summarises what each interim deliverable asked, did and found, with the evidence that survived into the hypothesis tree. It serves readers checking the evidence behind a Chapter 3 entry, and each section closes with a box naming the focus areas it supports. Chapter 3 takes the twenty focus areas in turn: the December hypothesis, its disposition, the evidence, what Wesgro does, what it asks of partners and what it escalates nationally. The Board and Exco can read it entry by entry and the programme owner in full; section 3.4 gives the sequence. Chapter 4 sets out which initiatives run, in what order, owned by whom, at what cost and with which decision gates, for the programme owner, Steerco and the partners named in the RACI. Chapter 5 sets out how progress is measured, through indicators, baselines, targets, data sources, the scorecard and the 2030 mid-term review, for Wesgro Research, the programme office and Steerco. Appendices A1 to A9 hold the traceability table, the demand model, the benchmark cases, readiness scores, the community fact base, stakeholder inputs, charters, the toolkit and references, for analysts and anyone checking a figure.

log.after: Each comparator's lesson translates into a change the Western Cape would have to make (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p20, p28, p35, p42, p49, p56). Chile's gateway-led air connectivity means treating air access as core economic infrastructure, with a permanent public-private air access fund and lobbying for air service liberalisation and simpler visas (p28). New Zealand's demand-engineered air access means ring-fencing marketing budgets around priority long-haul corridors, with an aviation partnership framework and early-stage route support (p56). Melbourne and Victoria's event-led demand means one event acquisition and calendar strategy across Wesgro, the Convention Bureau, the City and the Province, with conference bidding aligned to sector strengths (p20). Singapore's hub conversion and quality uplift means government, aviation, events and industry working to shared KPIs, under a province-wide quality and standards framework led by Wesgro (p42). Valencia's governed quality and sector councils mean a provincial quality charter phased by district, certification visible on booking platforms and standing sector councils for wine, MICE, adventure and culture (p49). Kenya's gateway diversification and conservation-led product mean treating MICE as a system lever, aligning city, provincial and national actors around a gateway strategy and building conservation and community inclusion into the offer (p35).

log.after: Cape Town's cruise berth has spare capacity, Mossel Bay is ready for day stops and Saldanha Bay is a watching brief (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, p110 to p112). Cape Town, where the stance is to protect, handled 83 calls and about 127,000 passengers in 2024/25, about 40% of a season capacity of 150 or more calls, for R1.79bn of impact; its limits are a 300m ship length, the South-Easter wind and no shore power. Saldanha Bay, to watch, has had 3 trial calls; it shares the ore terminal and has no cruise berth or passenger facility.

log.after: Each region carries a remaining gap that no committed investment closes (Infrastructure Report, Jul 2026, ratings p28, p41, p52, p63, p74, p85; gaps and investments p32, p43, p54, p65, p76, p87). The Cape Metro, rated 4.5, has the R11.3bn airport overhaul, the R20bn V&A Granger Bay expansion and the R3.3bn MyCiTi Phase 2. Last-mile transit to Chapman's Peak, Constantia and Cape Point, small-operator online booking and township product remain open. The Cape Winelands, rated 3.4, has the R8bn first phase of Cape Winelands Airport by 2028 and a wider precinct of R16bn to R20bn, but no transit inside the wine triangle, little non-wine product and no pricing for domestic visitors. The Garden Route, rated 3.4, has the R310m George terminal by 2028 and a R9.4m landing-system upgrade, but no international carrier, a winter trough and no transport between towns. The Overberg, rated 2.7, has the R81.7m Agulhas lighthouse precinct and the R17m Malgas road, but lacks accommodation towards De Hoop, bookability east of Hermanus and year-round product. The West Coast, rated 2.5, has the completed R693m Malmesbury bypass and the R4bn Saldanha port upgrade, which serves iron ore; it lacks accommodation depth and digital payments, and has no airport. The Central Karoo and Route 62, rated 1.9, have the R62 reconstruction under way and rural broadband to 2026, but lack accommodation depth and emergency support, and have no airport.

log.after: Five benchmark cases show that sellers outlast programmes and that capital without an operator earns nothing (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p7 to p11). In Santa Marta in Rio de Janeiro, about 20 resident guides ran the tours by 2015 and outside jeep firms had left: access and safety are preconditions, not product, and resident sellers outlast programmes (p7). Medellín's Comuna 13 drew 1.98 million visitors in 2025, 52% of them international, with about 300 professional guides; mobility built for residents became the stage, but carrying-capacity limits came late (p8). On Vilakazi Street in Soweto, ten restaurants employ more than 800 people; public-realm works amplify existing assets, but benefits concentrate on street-front owners (p9). Costa Rica's community network turned over more than USD 800,000 in 2013 and dissolved at the end of 2018: a selling entity is the engine and must survive donor exit (p10). Kliptown in Soweto received R436 million and drew about 4,000 museum visitors a year by 2017, because capital built before an operator yields no operating income (p11).

log.after: All six cases align coordination, marketing and access, but each builds its system around a different anchor (Global Benchmarking Report, Mar 2026, p61 for the system types; p59 to p60 for the three components, condensed). **Melbourne and Victoria: events-led.** Coordination institutionalises events and a knowledge-led brand as a cross-government economic development tool. Marketing integrates city branding, intellectual capital and events into a single demand proposition. The event calendar is used to de-risk and stimulate aviation demand. **Chile: connectivity-led.** Coordination is anchored around a single strategic constraint, long-haul access. Marketing runs unified national branding with defined regional identities and multi-region itinerary packaging. Liberal aviation policy and major hub investment position Santiago as a single efficient long-haul hub. **Kenya: product-led.** Coordination aligns tourism with national priorities in conservation, trade and diplomacy. Marketing is segment-specific and grounded in a designed product system. Access reduces entry friction, with Nairobi as a multipurpose regional and global hub. **Singapore: orchestrated experience.** A centrally orchestrated system under STB works through structured public-private partnerships. Marketing packages experiences (events, precincts, lifestyle) into seamless high-value propositions. Aviation, infrastructure and visitor experience are integrated into a single seamless gateway. **Valencia: governance-led.** Governance is decentralised and sector-led. Marketing expands the reasons to visit: gastronomy, culture, sport, wellness and business events. Connectivity supports a multi-product destination system and dispersal. **New Zealand: value-led.** Tourism, aviation and policy are integrated around shared demand objectives. Marketing shifts from volume to value by selling scarce, high-quality experiences. Long-haul demand converts only when marketing, aviation and distribution are aligned.

log.after: The plan finds that local selling mechanisms lasted while assets and training without a durable route to market did not, but Costa Rica's selling network did not survive donor exit (SME and Community Inclusion Plan, Sep 2026, p7 to p12, p30; the Rio, Medellín, Vilakazi Street and Kliptown cards print no source line, and the plan pools their sources on p12). **Rio de Janeiro, Santa Marta and Rocinha.** The Rio Top Tour's first phase cost about R$230,000 (R$184,000 federal, R$46,000 state). The Cantagalo elevator cost about R$89 million and the Providência cable car R$75 million in a R$163 million package, and almost 10,000 officers were deployed at peak (p7). The tours drew about 4,500 visitors in their first month in 2010, and about 20 resident guides were working by 2015. In 2014, 81% of foreign visitors spent up to R$10 in Rocinha. The cable car stood idle for eight years and security collapsed in 2017, yet Rocinha drew 544,000 visitors in 2023. Access and safety were preconditions, not product, and resident guides continued after the programme that launched them (p30). **Medellín, Comuna 13.** Metrocable Line J (2008) cost about 96.9 billion pesos and the escalators (2011) about 10 billion pesos, with maintenance above 260 million pesos a year; the integrated urban programme passed 100 billion pesos by 2020 (p8). Comuna 13 drew 1.66 million visitors in 2022 and 1.98 million in 2025, 52% of them international, with more than 1,000 businesses and about 300 guides. A 2023 study put its capacity at 667 visitors a day. The lesson is to fund a mandate, a capacity ceiling and a community body alongside the escalator; residents developed the product first (p30). **Soweto, Vilakazi Street.** The Hector Pieterson Museum cost R23.2 million, the Mandela House restoration about R9 million from corporate donors and Orlando Stadium about R280 million; the public-realm cost is not disclosed (p9). The street drew about 1,000 tourists a day by January 2010. Sakhumzi grew from four employees in 2001 to about 110 in 2019, and the ten restaurants provide more than 800 jobs, though the Mandela House company was liquidated. Upgrades amplified existing assets but benefits concentrated on street-front owners, so design governance and a resident precinct entity belong at the outset. **Costa Rica, ACTUAR.** UNDP GEF small grants funded the network from the 1990s. Law 8724 (2009) gave ICT duties without a budget, and no state funding for the selling network has been identified (p10). ACTUAR, founded in 2001, turned over more than USD 800,000 in 2013 for more than 30 member communities and dissolved at the end of 2018; its benefits "stopped at association members". A management entity with its own selling channel was the engine, and it did not survive donor exit. **Soweto, Kliptown.** Kliptown received R436 million in its first allocation. The JDA spent about R497 million from 2001 to 2010 plus R40 million to 2013, Walter Sisulu Square cost R160 million to R180 million and a 48-room hotel R24 million (p11). The business case projected almost 200,000 international visitors a year, but the museum drew about 4,000 a year by 2017 and the hotel traded above break-even only during the 2010 FIFA World Cup. Local small businesses took 5% of construction contract value, and the site was looted in 2021. Heritage converts to local income only when operator, trader and guide product, security and services are funded before the ribbon is cut.
